newsitem.title: USA: Clinton says U.S. strong, but sees challenges.
newsitem.headline: Clinton says U.S. strong, but sees challenges.

text.p: President Bill Clinton previewed his State of the Union speech on Monday, telling U.S. governors at a White House meeting the nation is strong, at peace and prosperous but faces many challenges.

"This is an unusual opportunity for our country and for every state," Clinton told the governors, who are in the midst of their annual Washington conference. "The nation is strong, we are at peace, we have extraordinary prosperity."
"But we know we're living through a time of great change. There are significant challenges which if not faced will have destructive conseqeunces for our nation in the years ahead.

"So as we stand on the edge of this new century and this profoundly new era, we have a unique opportunity and a common responsibility -- which is to take action together to try to prepare this country not just for the next four years, but for the next fifty years," he said.

Clinton is scheduled to deliver the annual televised State of the Union address, laying out a broad overview of where the nation stands and where it should be headed, to Congress at 9 p.m. EST on Tuesday (0200 GMT on Wednesday).

The president's approval ratings are holding steady at 60 percent ahead of the speech, while only 36 percent of Americans approve of the way Congress is handling its job, according to a new CNN/USA Today/Gallup poll released on Monday.

Clinton told the governors his speech would discuss a number of "challenges," including implementing the welfare reform law that he signed last year ending the 61-year-old federal guarantee of aid to the poor.

Many of the contentious topics that he discussed with the governors on Monday -- including trimming the Medicaid health care programme for the poor and restoring spending on some benefits to legal immigrants -- may also come up.

Aides said Clinton spent a part of the weekend working on the speech and, after a brief meeting with Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori, was likely to spend much of Monday and Tuesday doing the same.
"The speech is in very good shape," spokesman Mike McCurry said. "He may have a couple of things he'll do tomorrow but by and large it'll be working through the speech."

The annual review is mandated by the Constitution, which says the president "shall from time to time give to the Congress information of the State of the Union, and recommend to their consideration such measures as he shall judge necessary and expedient."
Such speeches often disappear into history unnoticed. Clinton last year grabbed some attention with his blunt statement that "The era of big government is over."
This year officials have said there are unlikely to be surprises in the speech, saying Clinton would present the ideas he ran on in last year's campaign in a detailed fashion.

Clinton, who began a second four-year term as U.S. chief executive on Jan. 20, ran on a platform of balancing the budget by 2002, raising the level of education, moving poor people from welfare to work and keeping the economy strong.
On Thursday, he was scheduled to send his new budget to Congress, further fleshing out his agenda for the nation.
Gallup polled 1,056 Americans between Jan. 31 and Feb. 2 for its latest poll, which has a margin of error of plus or minus three percentage points.
